newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - Good global economic prospects - T.Roehm.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Good global economic prospects - T.Roehm.

text.p: By Thomas Roehm, Economist at the Ifo economic research institute in Munich

The upward trend in the global economy is continuing. This was demonstrated by the Economic Survey International (ESI) of about 450 economists in 67 countries carried out by the Ifo institute for economic research in April.
The economic climate continues to be favourable and the current economic situation and prospects for the next six months were positively evaluated in most countries.
The economic development in the first quarter of 1997 was better than expected, particularly in the USA and Britain.
In Japan, too, where the mood at the beginning of the year threw up doubts as to the permanence of the economic recovery, the evaluation of the current economic situation was better.
The development in continental Europe was disappointing, where low interest rates and competitive exchange rates suggested a quick recovery as early as the beginning of the year.
A slight decline is expected in the USA in the second and third quarters of 1997, as the majority of companies are working close to their capacity limits and further interest rate rises are expected.
In total though, the real GDP growth rate should reach a level of 2.7 percent, slightly above the previous year's rate of 2.4 percent.
In Britain, the brisker capital goods demand - compared to the first quarter - should ensure the continuation of high growth for the coming half year.

Of the other western European countries, the northern lights -- Ireland, Finland and Norway in particular -- continue to have favorable growth prospects and in these countries the GDP growth rate for the whole year should lie well above the western European average of 2.3 percent.
The economic situation in France, Italy, Belgium, Switzerland and Germany is still unsatisfactory.

Hopes for an improvement in the next six months in Germany, Italy and Switzerland rely on a strong increase in exports. As, according to the experts asked, the dollar is going to remain strong, the prospects for this are favourable.
With growth rates of around 2.3 percent, the upturn in most western European countries compared to the previous year should be consolidated.
The only exception is Switzerland, whose economy is likely to stagnate this year following a decline of 0.7 percent in the previous year.

The majority of Asian countries are also increasingly reliant on experts. This is particularly the case for Japan, where weak private consumer demand (among other things, V.A.T. was increased in Spring) is dampening growth, but also for most of the emerging economies.

Last year, several of these countries experienced cuts in growth due to the declining export demand from industrial countries. In addition, in countries like Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia domestic demand was reduced due to restrictive financial policy intended to combat signs of overheating.
Now, the majority of countries are regaining their self-confidence (Korea is the only country where an improvement is not expected in the next few months).
The economic climate in India has significantly improved since the beginning of the year.
The Asian countries have the most favourable growth forecasts for 1997 worldwide. On average, a GDP increase of 5.2 percent is expected in Asia.

In China, GDP is expected to expand strongly, provisionally by almost 10 percent. Stable prices complete the picture of the Chinese economy's "soft landing", annual inflation for 1997 should be about 6 percent like in the previous year.
In Latin America as well the growth prospects have significantly improved. The economy expanded more strongly than expected in 1996.

After the peso crisis in Mexico and Argentina in 1995 had caused a severe slump and pessimistic expectations, the economy in both countries was able to grow strongly again in 1996 (5.1 and 4.4 percent).

While GDP growth in Mexico may decline slightly in 1997 (4.7 percent), the Argentinian economy is expected to continue to grow (5.4 percent). Venezuela should experience a recovery in 1997, the expected rate of GDP growth is, like in Brazil, significantly over 3 percent.

The economic development in the central and eastern European countries remains moderate. Of the countries more advanced in transition, probably only Poland (over 5 percent growth) and the Czech Republic (around 4 percent) will be able to sustain fast economic growth.
The forecasts for the Slovak Republic for 1997 at 3.3 percent growth are still significantly lower than in the previous year (GDP increased by 7 percent in 1996).

A slight revival is apparent in Hungary at the moment, but a growth rate of just 2 percent is expected for the whole year. The economic development in the Baltic states continues to be steady with growth rates of 3 percent. In contrast, economic performance in Russia in 1997 is expected to fall off slightly.
The situation on the financial and currency markets is still characterised by price level stability and low interest rates as well as generally favourably economic prospects.
Now that the leading interest rates have been raised in Britain and then in the USA, higher interest rates are to be expected in most other industrial nations.
The long-term interest rates which up until the beginning of 1997 were mostly falling, have since then started to rise again slightly in many industrialised countries.
While in the USA this development was caused by growing fear of inflation, in Europe uncertainties connected with the European Monetary Union played a part.

On the foreign exchange markets the strong dollar will almost certainly be able to assert itself for the time being. The experts asked increasingly classified the British pound as overvalued. In contrast, the Japanese yen shows a definite tendency to undervaluation.
